source.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
source.authors: Jordan Hoffmann; Sebastian Borgeaud; Arthur Mensch; Elena Buchatskaya; Trevor Cai; Eliza Rutherford; D. de Las Casas; Lisa Anne Hendricks; Johannes Welbl; Aidan Clark; T. Hennigan; Eric Noland; Katie Millican; George van den Driessche; Bogdan Damoc; Aurelia Guy; Simon Osindero; K. Simonyan; Erich Elsen; Jack W. Rae; O. Vinyals; L. Sifre

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains language models and uses multiple loss-fitting and compute-allocation analyses to examine scaling, but does not reproduce Kaplan et al.'s exact fitting setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling and language-model loss results, plus extensive downstream evaluations. Downstream task scores are not separately recorded because they do not directly measure held-out pretraining loss or the loss-minimising allocation. Results cited from Kaplan et al. are not treated as study results.
record.test_reason: This is an original source (Hoffmann et al.). Its own results directly estimate the loss law (V1), the compute-optimal allocation (V3) and fit sensitivity (V7) with the method that defines the claim. As an original source it gets no verdict labels.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also state that the C4 and GitHub results suggest the allocation is dataset-independent under one epoch. They add that concavity in the frontier means optimal large-model sizes may still be overestimated.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses training-curve envelopes, IsoFLOP profiles, and a parametric loss fit rather than Kaplan et al.'s fixed-token and fixed-schedule setup. It argues that matching the cosine schedule to the training horizon changes loss estimates.
record.method_sensitivity: The cosine cycle length affects training loss; schedules more than 25% longer than the target impair performance. Larger Huber δ values overfit the small-compute regime and poorly predict held-out larger runs, while δ below 10−3 does not change predictions. The fitted approaches give somewhat different allocation exponents, and the frontier shows curvature.
record.peer_reviewed: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022)
record.problems: The authors report only two comparable training runs at large scale (Chinchilla and Gopher), no repeated Chinchilla run, and no additional tests at intermediate scales. The scaling analysis assumes a power-law compute/model relationship despite observed curvature. The scaling runs use less than an epoch of data, and the authors note that the language-model comparison may be affected by train/test leakage because Chinchilla saw more data.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Downstream-task scores were not included because they do not directly measure the claim's pretraining-loss scaling or loss-minimising allocation.

untested.parts: No small-run fit is used to predict the numeric loss of a much larger run. Only the Huber-δ remark (larger δ predicts held-out larger runs poorly) touches this.
No controlled depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
Only text datasets (MassiveText, C4, GitHub) are used. Training is under one epoch, with no repeated data, fine-tuning or other modalities.
Downstream gains of Chinchilla over Gopher are reported, but there is no test of predictability from scale or loss.
No separate compute-only power law. The parametric L(N,D) fit is on smoothed training loss.

missing.what: Head-to-head at 1e21 FLOPs: a 2.80B model (Approach 1 optimum) beats a 4.74B model (Kaplan optimum) in final training loss.
FLOP counting including embeddings versus the 6ND approximation. Ratios run 0.99–1.10, and the authors say this does not affect the analysis.
Approach 3 predicts much larger token counts than Approaches 1–2 at large budgets (e.g. 4.1T vs 1.5–1.7T tokens for 67B), showing that the choice of fitting method matters.

record.verdict_notes: This paper is an original source for V3, so no verdict labels are given. Its rows serve as the reference against which other studies are compared. The A1–A5 exponents (a=0.46–0.53) bear on V3 (near-equal scaling) and, through their spread across methods and datasets, on V7. The record's reader-assigned tranche T2 is changed to T1 because this is the defining study.

versions.untested_parts: The paper fits a loss function with parameter- and data-dependent power terms, using smoothed training loss as an unbiased test-loss estimate; it does not separately establish a power law in compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
The study predicts an optimal parameter/token allocation and trains Chinchilla to test that allocation; it does not report a small-run-fitted prediction of a larger run's held-out pretraining loss.

The study estimates the compute-optimal parameter and token scaling exponents and tests a predicted allocation at Gopher's compute budget. It does not test optimal allocation across all model sizes or compute budgets.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
C4 and GitHub are alternative text datasets, not other modalities or the listed training regimes such as repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports downstream comparisons but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
The study reports sensitivity to schedule and fitting choices and curvature in the compute frontier, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions or all data and schedule choices.

rows.subject: Over 400 language models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a parametric loss function to losses from Approaches 1 and 2.
rows.measure: Fitted loss as a function of parameter count N and training tokens D
rows.note: The paper says it analyzes smoothed training loss as an unbiased estimate of test loss in the infinite-data regime.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3; Appendix D.2, Equation (10); introduction footnote 2.

rows.subject: Over 400 language models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit power laws to the minimum-loss-per-FLOP envelope from training curves.
rows.measure: Optimal parameter count and training tokens versus compute exponents
rows.uncertainty: 10th and 90th percentiles: N exponent (0.488, 0.502); D exponent (0.501, 0.512)
rows.note: The exponents describe the paper's estimated compute-optimal allocation.

source_check.correct: Approach 1 uses models ranging from 70M to approximately 10B parameters, each trained for four horizons. The over-400 count and approximately 16B upper size describe the combined study, not this approach alone. Exponents remain 0.50/0.50.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1; Figure 2 caption; Section 3.2 footnote 5; Table 2.

rows.note: The paper reports similar scaling behavior to its MassiveText analysis.

rows.subject: Models in the cosine-cycle-length experiment (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Vary cosine cycle length relative to the target number of training steps.
rows.measure: Training loss under mismatched schedule lengths
rows.baseline: Cosine cycle length matched to target training steps
rows.value: Overestimating training steps beyond 25% leads to clear drops in performance.
rows.note: The paper says a cycle that is too long impairs performance because the learning rate does not drop appropriately.
rows.check: Recorded as partial. Figure A1 and Appendix D.1 clearly show that cycles more than 25% too long degrade loss, and Section 2 ties this schedule choice to Kaplan's different allocation. The effect V7 names appears in full.

rows.subject: Over 400 language models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: under 70 million to over 16 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Examine curvature in the FLOP-minimal loss frontier and fit portions of the frontier separately.
rows.measure: Curvature of the loss frontier and resulting optimal-size projections
rows.value: The paper reports curvature/concavity in the frontier; projections from very small models differ from those from larger models, and the curvature may mean larger optimal sizes are overestimated.
rows.note: The authors say the observed concavity in log Nopt at high compute budgets is not incorporated in their analysis.
rows.check: Recorded as partial. Appendix E and Section 3.4 report negative curvature in the frontier, and fits on different thirds give different projections. This is the bending V7 describes. The paper calls it 'slight' but does not treat it as absent.

rows.subject: Over 400 language models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: under 70 million to over 16 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Vary the Huber-loss fitting parameter δ in the parametric loss fit.
rows.measure: Fit behavior and prediction on larger-compute held-out data
rows.value: Larger δ values overfit the small-compute regime and poorly predict held-out data from larger runs; δ below 10−3 does not impact resulting predictions.
rows.note: A specific fitting choice changes the behavior of the fitted loss model.

rows.subject: Chinchilla (70B)
rows.operation_detail: Train a model at the predicted compute-optimal allocation and compare its held-out language-model loss with Gopher at equal training compute.
rows.note: Chinchilla used 1.4 trillion tokens; Gopher used 300 billion. The paper cautions that greater training data may increase train/test leakage.
rows.check: Confounded comparison. Chinchilla also differs from Gopher in optimiser (AdamW vs Adam), tokenizer and data mix (Section 4.1, Appendix G). The authors also caution about train/test leakage.
